title: 7 Best Exterior Caulks in 2026: Matched to Joint and Surface
metaDescription: DAP Dynaflex 230 is the best exterior caulk for most painted homes. 7 picks for windows, siding, brick and metal, sorted by movement and paintability.
keywords: best caulk for exterior windows and doors
best paintable caulk for outdoor use
best exterior caulk for wood siding
best caulk for exterior metal siding holes
intro:
The best exterior caulk for most painted houses is DAP Dynaflex 230, an elastomeric latex that cleans up with water, takes paint and stretches far more than cheap painter's caulk. For windows with bare glass or metal, vinyl siding, brick and roof-edge metal, a different chemistry wins, and this guide names the tube for each.

Most failed beads are not bad caulk. They are the wrong chemistry for the joint: stiff acrylic stretched across a moving siding joint, or silicone run along trim that later got painted. Below you will find seven picks, how to read a label, how deep a joint should be, cold-weather limits and how long each type lasts.
quickAnswer: Buy DAP Dynaflex 230 for painted siding, trim and window perimeters. Use Sashco Big Stretch where joints keep cracking, OSI Quad Advanced on vinyl and fiber cement, Geocel 2300 on metal and masonry, and GE Advanced Silicone 2 on glass and metal that will never be painted. Whatever you buy, cut out the old bead first and size deep joints with backer rod.

sections.heading: Best Exterior Caulk: The Short Answer
sections.body:
| Pick | Best for | Key spec |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DAP Dynaflex 230 | Most painted siding, trim and window joints | Elastomeric latex, paintable, water cleanup |
| Sashco Big Stretch | Joints that keep cracking open | Water-based elastomeric, stretches several times its width per Sashco |
| OSI Quad Advanced | Vinyl, fiber cement and siding trim | Solvent-style polymer, siding-matched colors |
| GE Advanced Silicone 2 Window and Door | Glass, aluminum, unpainted metal | 100% silicone, not paintable |
| Geocel 2300 | Metal, masonry and roof-edge joints | Solvent-based tripolymer, paintable after cure |
| Loctite Polyseamseal | Small, stable gaps on a budget | Acrylic adhesive caulk |
| DAP Alex Plus | Cosmetic touch-ups on painted trim | Siliconized acrylic latex |

If the joint will be painted, choose elastomeric latex or a paintable polymer. If the joint will never be painted and takes a lot of water, choose silicone. Then let the surfaces on both sides of the joint narrow it down: vinyl and fiber cement point to a polymer, brick and metal to a tripolymer, glass to silicone.

Movement levels in the table are relative, based on each chemistry family and how the maker positions the product. Check the back of the tube for the ASTM class before you buy.

sections.heading: The 7 Best Exterior Caulks in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
These are ordered by how many joints on a typical house each tube handles well, so the lower picks are specialists, not weaker products. The ranking draws on what each maker publishes (ASTM movement class, rated substrates, temperature limits, paintability, warranty) and on problems that come up again and again in owner reports. No lab rig was involved and no scores were invented.

### Best Overall: DAP Dynaflex 230

Dynaflex 230 is the tube to start with on a painted house. It is an elastomeric latex sealant, which means it works and cleans up like ordinary latex caulk but stretches much further once it cures. That extra give is what lets it survive trim-to-siding joints, corner boards and window and door perimeters that open and close with the seasons.

DAP lists adhesion to wood, vinyl, aluminum, brick and fiber cement, backs it with a lifetime durability claim, and sells it in a long run of factory colors. It is gun grade, so it comes out of a standard 10.1 oz cartridge in a smooth, controllable bead, and it accepts latex or oil paint after a short wait. Two latex habits still apply. It is not made to sit under standing water, and like every water-based sealant it loses a little volume as it cures, so a deep gap needs backer rod rather than a fat bead. For most houses that get painted every several years, this is the one tube that covers the majority of joints.

**Pros:** water cleanup, paints well, flexible through freeze-thaw, grips most siding and trim materials, many colors.

**Cons:** not for joints that hold standing water; shrinks a little on deep fills.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DAP+Dynaflex+230&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Joints That Keep Cracking: Sashco Big Stretch

Big Stretch exists for the joint that splits open every spring no matter what you put in it. Sashco markets it on stretch: the company says the cured bead can extend to several times its own width, which is far beyond what a standard acrylic can follow. Owners commonly report it holding where wood trim meets brick, on long butt joints in lap siding and on log homes, all places where cheap caulk tore within a season.

It is water based, low odor and paintable, so it slots into a normal repaint. The tradeoff is handling. It comes out sticky and tends to string off the nozzle, so tooling is slower and messier than with Dynaflex. Keep a damp rag and a tooling stick in reach and work short runs. It also shrinks visibly in wide, deep joints as the water leaves, which is one more reason to fill depth with foam rod first. If your problem spots are a hot south wall or wood rubbing against masonry, the extra fuss is worth it.

**Pros:** exceptional stretch, paintable, low odor, water cleanup, holds up in heat and cold.

**Cons:** stringy and sticky to tool; noticeable shrinkage in wide joints.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Sashco+Big+Stretch+caulk&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Vinyl and Fiber Cement Siding: OSI Quad Advanced Formula

Siding installers have used OSI Quad for years because it bites into surfaces that latex struggles with, vinyl and coated metal above all. The Advanced Formula is the current version, sold for window, door and siding perimeters in a long list of colors matched to common siding shades. That color range matters if you never plan to paint the joint.

Quad is a solvent-style polymer, not a water-based product. Expect stickier tooling and cleanup with the solvent the label names rather than a wet rag. In return it is more tolerant than latex of a slightly damp joint or a cool morning, and it keeps its grip on vinyl as the panels slide back and forth with temperature. It also accepts paint if you want it to. OSI has revised the formula over time, so check the tube you buy for its exact temperature window and cure guidance. For vinyl, fiber cement and aluminum trim, this is the safer bet than any latex.

**Pros:** strong grip on vinyl, fiber cement, aluminum and wood; paintable; tolerates damp surfaces; siding-matched colors.

**Cons:** harder to tool and clean up than latex; costs more per tube than basic caulk.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=OSI+Quad+Advanced+window+door+siding+sealant&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Pure Silicone for Windows and Glass: GE Advanced Silicone 2 Window and Door

For glass, aluminum and other nonporous surfaces, 100 percent silicone is still the most weatherproof option a homeowner can buy, and GE Advanced Silicone 2 is the version most hardware stores keep on the shelf. GE markets the window and door line as shrink and crack proof and rain ready a short time after application, which is useful when a storm is due that evening.

Its sweet spot is glass to frame, vinyl and aluminum window flanges, metal flashing and gutter-adjacent trim. The limits are firm. Paint will not stick to it, so it is wrong for any joint you plan to paint. It bonds less reliably to raw wood and masonry than a polymer or elastomeric latex. And cured silicone leaves a film that almost nothing else bonds to, so the next recaulk takes serious scrubbing. If you are sealing a modern glass pane into a wood frame and the wood side will be painted, use a paintable polymer instead. Where the joint stays unpainted and takes a lot of water, this is the right tube.

**Pros:** fully waterproof once cured, excellent UV resistance, rain ready quickly per the label, stays flexible for years.

**Cons:** cannot be painted; weak on porous wood and masonry; old residue is hard to remove.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=GE+Advanced+Silicone+2+window+door+sealant&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Metal and Masonry: Geocel 2300 Construction Tripolymer

Geocel 2300 is the contractor fix for the surface that is less than ideal. It is a solvent-based tripolymer sold for metal roofing, flashing, masonry and siding joints, and its reputation rests on grabbing surfaces that are a bit damp, chalky or oily, where a water-based caulk would peel. That makes it a strong match for brick-to-trim joints, chimney flashing edges, metal sheds and seams near gutters.

The cured bead stays rubbery and handles large joint movement, and it takes paint after cure, though plenty of people leave it in one of its stock colors. It also works on cooler days than most latex. The price is the application experience. It smells strongly of solvent, strings off the nozzle and sticks to gloves, so plan to work slowly with mineral spirits at hand for cleanup. It is overkill for small interior-style gaps on trim, but for the joint between brick and wood or the metal seam that has already failed twice, it is the tube to buy.

**Pros:** bonds to damp and slightly dirty surfaces, very strong on metal and masonry, handles big movement, paintable after cure, works in cool weather.

**Cons:** strong solvent odor; messy, stringy application; mineral spirits cleanup.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Geocel+2300+tripolymer+sealant&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Budget Pick: Loctite Polyseamseal All Purpose Adhesive Caulk

Polyseamseal is a long-running acrylic adhesive caulk that sits between a bargain painter's caulk and a true elastomeric sealant. It grips better than the cheapest latex tubes, which helps on small gaps where two materials meet, and it still cleans up with water and takes paint.

That makes it a fair buy for a large number of small, stable joints: nail-hole runs along trim, short gaps between window casing and stucco that barely move, and the edges around fixture and pipe penetrations. Where it falls behind is stretch. It is not formulated to extend the way Dynaflex, Big Stretch or the polymers do, so on long butt joints, wide corner boards or any joint on a sunny wall that cycles hard, expect cracking sooner. The smart way to use it is as a budget stretcher: put it on the easy, sheltered joints and spend the savings on a premium sealant for the joints that face weather and move.

**Pros:** low price per tube, water cleanup, paintable, better grip than basic acrylic.

**Cons:** much less movement capacity than elastomeric or polymer sealants; wrong for large or high-stress joints.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Loctite+Polyseamseal+all+purpose+adhesive+caulk&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Painted Trim Touch-Ups: DAP Alex Plus

Alex Plus is the caulk most garages already hold, and it earns a spot here for a narrow job. It is a siliconized acrylic latex, labeled for interior and exterior use, that tools to a smooth, paint-ready finish with a wet finger and takes paint quickly. The silicone additive improves flexibility and adhesion compared with plain acrylic.

Outdoors, that makes it fine for cosmetic gaps on painted trim: the hairline between a casing and its backband, nail holes in fascia, a short miter that never moves. It is not a primary weather seal on a joint that works. Owners who run it along siding butt joints, long horizontal trim boards or a south wall commonly see it crack within a season or two, and that is the product doing what its limited movement rating predicts. Keep a tube for paint prep and quick fixes, and reach for an elastomeric or polymer sealant for every joint that actually keeps water out of the wall.

**Pros:** inexpensive and sold everywhere, very easy to tool smooth, paints fast, fine on narrow stable gaps.

**Cons:** limited movement outdoors; cracks early on sunny walls and long joints; not a primary weather seal.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DAP+Alex+Plus+caulk&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: What Is the Best Caulk for Exterior Windows?
sections.body:
For a painted wood or composite window, an elastomeric latex such as Dynaflex 230 or a paintable polymer such as OSI Quad is the best exterior window caulk. For a joint between glass and a frame, or around an aluminum or vinyl flange that will stay unpainted, 100 percent silicone is the better choice.

### Which window joints to seal

Seal the joint where the window casing or brick mould meets the siding, the head and side joints of the trim, and any gap where a sill meets the wall. These are the paths rain follows into the wall. If you are setting a modern glass pane into a wood sash, the glazing side usually wants silicone or a glazing compound, while the painted wood side wants a paintable sealant.

### Which window joints to leave open

Leave the weep slots at the bottom of the frame and any drainage gaps the window maker designed in. Many installations also leave the bottom edge of the nailing flange unsealed on purpose so water that gets behind the trim can drain out. Caulking those shut traps water inside the wall, which is far worse than a small leak you can see.

### One tube per window

A standard double-hung window perimeter runs about 18 to 20 feet, and a 10.1 oz tube fills about 24 feet of a quarter-inch joint. That makes one tube per window a fair planning number. While you are up there, check that gutters above the window drain properly; overflowing gutters dump water down the wall and overwhelm the joints, which is where a set of [gutter guards](/best-gutter-guards/) can help.

sections.heading: Silicone, Latex or Polymer: Which Type Is Best Outdoors?
sections.body:
Elastomeric latex or a paintable polymer is best for anything you will paint, and 100 percent silicone is best for unpainted joints that take heavy water. The chemistry on the back of the tube predicts behavior much better than the brand on the front.

### The five families

| Chemistry | Typical movement | Paintable | Cleanup | Best use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Acrylic latex | Low | Yes, fast | Water | Stable painted trim gaps |
| Elastomeric latex | Moderate to high | Yes | Water | Painted siding and trim joints |
| 100% silicone | High | No | Solvent | Glass, metal, unpainted joints |
| Polyurethane or hybrid polymer | High | Yes | Solvent or as labeled | Vinyl, fiber cement, masonry |
| Tripolymer | High | Yes, after cure | Mineral spirits | Metal, roofing, damp masonry |

Basic acrylic latex is cheap and easy, but its stretch is small, which is fine indoors and poor on siding. Elastomeric latex keeps the easy cleanup and stretches several times further. Silicone is the most water and UV resistant, which is why people searching for a UV resistant caulk usually end up with it, but it cannot be painted. Polymers and tripolymers cost more and are harder to clean up, and they are what pros use on vinyl, fiber cement, metal and brick.

### Butyl rubber

Butyl stays tacky, picks up dirt and firms up very slowly, so skip it on any joint people will see. It still has a place on gutter seams and metal roof laps.

sections.heading: How Do You Read an Exterior Caulk Label?
sections.body:
Look for the ASTM standard first. It is the one number on the tube that tells you how far the bead can stretch.

### ASTM C834 vs ASTM C920

ASTM C834 covers latex sealants and sets a low bar for movement. A tube that lists only C834 is, for outdoor purposes, a painter's caulk. ASTM C920 covers elastomeric joint sealants and adds a class number. Class 25 means the sealant is built to handle movement of plus or minus 25 percent of the joint width; Class 35 and Class 50 handle more. You may also see NS, for non-sag, which means the bead will stay put in a vertical joint.

### What that means for a real joint

A 3/8-inch joint between two wood boards on a sunny wall can open and close by a sixteenth of an inch or more over a year. That is about 17 percent of its width: inside a Class 25 rating and beyond what basic latex can follow. Wider joints are more forgiving because the same movement is a smaller share of the width, which is why sealant makers discourage joints narrower than about a quarter inch.

### Three more numbers

After movement, find the minimum application temperature, the rain-ready time and the paint-ready time. Those three decide whether you can do the job this weekend. If the tube is vague, the maker's technical data sheet will list them.

sections.heading: What Caulk Works on Wood Siding, Vinyl, Brick and Metal?
sections.body:
Name the material on both sides of the joint before you shop. The harder of the two decides the product.

### Wood siding and trim

Painted wood is the easiest surface. Elastomeric latex such as Dynaflex 230 or Big Stretch grips it, takes paint and keeps up with seasonal swelling. Exterior caulks for butt joints and trim should carry a C920 class, because butt joints in long boards move more than any other joint on the house. Never caulk over soft or rotted wood; cut the rot out and rebuild it with a product from our [wood filler guide](/best-wood-filler/) first. If you are finishing bare wood rather than painting it, see the [exterior wood sealer picks](/best-exterior-wood-sealer/) for what goes on after the caulk.

### Vinyl, fiber cement and composite

Vinyl moves a lot with temperature and has a slick face that latex struggles to hold. A polymer such as OSI Quad is the safer choice. Do not caulk the laps where vinyl panels lock together; they need to slide and drain. Fiber cement makers set their own sealant requirements in the installation instructions, usually a paintable sealant meeting ASTM C920, so read those first.

### Brick, stone and stucco

Masonry is porous, alkaline and often dusty. Polymer and tripolymer sealants such as Geocel 2300 hold it much better than latex. Wire-brush the joint edges first, and never seal brick weep holes.

### Metal siding, flashing and glass

For holes and seams in metal siding that will be painted, use a paintable polymer or tripolymer. For unpainted metal, aluminum flanges and glass, use 100 percent silicone.

sections.heading: How Cold Is Too Cold to Caulk Outside?
sections.body:
Most water-based caulks list a minimum of about 40 degrees Fahrenheit, and that applies to the surface as well as the air. Polymer and solvent-based sealants usually allow colder application, and some are labeled for use near freezing. A north wall at dawn in October can sit several degrees below the forecast, so check the surface itself.

### Application limit vs service limit

These are separate numbers. The service range is the weather a cured bead can live through. The application minimum is what it needs from the moment you gun it until it skins over. A sealant that shrugs off a hard winter once cured can still fail if it went onto a frosty surface.

### The best time to caulk

Spring and fall, mid-morning to mid-afternoon, on dry surfaces between roughly 50 and 80 degrees, with no rain for at least the window on the tube. A joint sealed at a middling temperature is at a middling width, so the bead stretches and compresses by similar amounts as the seasons change.

Avoid a dark wall in full summer sun. The joint is at its narrowest then, so the bead spends winter stretched hard, and the hot surface skins the caulk before you can tool it. If the job cannot wait, follow the shade around the house.

### Hot, sunny climates

In high-sun regions UV breaks down latex binders and leaves a chalky, cracked bead on south and west walls within a few years. For unpainted joints, silicone is the most UV-stable choice. On painted joints, a solid coat of exterior acrylic paint over the sealant shields it and adds years.

sections.heading: How Deep Should Exterior Caulk Be, and When Do You Need Backer Rod?
sections.body:
Aim for sealant about half as deep as the joint is wide, with a practical minimum of about a quarter inch, and fill anything deeper with closed-cell foam backer rod first.

| Joint width | Target sealant depth | Backer rod |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1/4 inch | 1/4 inch | Usually none |
| 3/8 inch | 1/4 inch | 1/2-inch rod if deep |
| 1/2 inch | 1/4 inch | 5/8-inch rod |
| 3/4 inch | 3/8 inch | 1-inch rod |
| Over 1 inch | Not recommended | Rebuild the joint |

### Why shape matters

A movement rating only holds when the bead is wider than it is deep and sticks to the two sides of the gap but not the back. That hourglass profile stretches evenly like a rubber band. A bead stuck to three sides cannot, and it tears along the edges.

### Using rod and tape

Pick a rod about 25 percent wider than the gap so it stays put, press it in with a blunt tool and do not puncture it, since punctured closed-cell rod can off-gas and blister the sealant. Where a joint is too shallow for rod, such as lap siding against a corner board, a strip of bond-breaker tape on the bottom does the same job. Once a gap passes about an inch, caulk is the wrong repair: add trim or flashing, then seal the narrower joint that remains.

sections.heading: How Do You Caulk Exterior Joints So the Bead Lasts?
sections.body:
Remove the old bead, clean to bare surfaces, push a properly sized bead into the joint and tool it before it skins. Each step is short, and skipping any of them shortens the life of even the best tube.

### Step by step

1. **Cut out the old caulk.** Slice both edges with a sharp blade or hooked removal tool and scrape off the rest. New caulk over old bonds only to material that is already failing.
2. **Clean and dry.** Brush out dust and paint flakes, wipe the edges with isopropyl alcohol and let them dry. Treat mildew with a diluted bleach solution, rinse and dry. Scrub any old silicone film with a silicone remover.
3. **Cut the nozzle and push.** Cut at about 45 degrees with an opening slightly smaller than the joint, and push the bead ahead of the nozzle so sealant is driven into the gap. A dripless gun with a smooth thrust ratio helps a lot.
4. **Tool right away.** Use a tooling spoon or wet finger to press the sealant against both sides and leave a slightly concave face. For crisp lines, tape both sides and pull the tape just after tooling.
5. **Work short runs.** About three feet at a time in warm weather, especially with fast-skinning silicone and polymers. Wipe smears at once with water or the labeled solvent.

### Rain and paint timing

Labels list rain-ready times from under an hour for some silicones to several hours for latex. Latex usually takes paint within an hour or two up to a day; polymers often need longer, and silicone never takes paint. Full cure takes several days for latex and a week or more for a thick polymer bead. Topcoat with exterior acrylic paint, carried a few millimeters past each edge, rather than stiffer oil paint.

sections.heading: How Long Does Exterior Caulk Last, and How Many Tubes Do You Need?
sections.body:
Plain acrylic on a sunny wall may last only a few years, a good elastomeric latex under paint commonly lasts much longer, and many silicone and polymer sealants carry multi-decade durability claims on the label. Those claims assume correct joint size, backer rod where needed and a bead laid on bare, clean surfaces.

### Signs it is time to recaulk

Walk the house each spring and fall. Replace a bead that has pulled away from one side, cracked through, turned hard and brittle, or shrunk until you can see daylight. Fine crazing in paint over a bead is often cosmetic; press it with a fingernail, and if the sealant underneath is still rubbery and attached on both sides, fresh paint may be all it needs.

### How much to buy

| Bead size | Approx. feet per 10.1 oz tube | Typical job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1/8 x 1/8 inch | about 90 feet | Hairline trim gaps |
| 1/4 x 1/4 inch | about 24 feet | Window and door perimeters |
| 3/8 x 1/4 inch | about 16 feet | Siding to trim |
| 1/2 x 1/4 inch | about 12 feet | Wide trim joints with rod |

Add up window and door perimeters, corner boards, butt joints and penetrations, divide by the coverage for your usual bead and add 20 percent for waste. Most whole houses need somewhere between 10 and 20 tubes. Spend on premium sealant for the joints that face weather and move, and save budget acrylic for small, sheltered, painted gaps. Avoid big 28 oz cartridges unless the job is continuous, because an opened cartridge cures within days.

Caulk is one part of keeping water out. Pair it with protected wood, such as a good [fence stain](/best-fence-stain/) or deck finish, and gutters that actually carry water away.

mistakes.title: Using painter's caulk on siding joints
mistakes.body: Cheap acrylic that lists only ASTM C834 has very little stretch. On butt joints, corner boards and sunny walls the joint moves further than the bead can follow, and it cracks within a season or two. Any joint that works needs an elastomeric latex or polymer with an ASTM C920 movement class.

mistakes.title: Caulking over the old bead
mistakes.body: A fresh bead laid on a failing one sticks only to the old material, so both layers peel off together within months. Cut out the old sealant completely, scrape the residue, clean both edges and lay the new bead against bare, sound surfaces.

mistakes.title: Filling deep gaps with sealant alone
mistakes.body: A bead deeper than it is wide cannot stretch evenly, shrinks as it cures, eats tubes and usually bonds to the back of the joint. Press in closed-cell backer rod about a quarter wider than the gap so the sealant ends up roughly half as deep as the joint is wide.

mistakes.title: Running silicone where paint is planned
mistakes.body: Paint beads up and peels on silicone, and silicone residue keeps contaminating the joint after the bead is cut out. If a joint might ever be painted, start with a paintable elastomeric or polymer, and keep silicone for glass, metal and joints that will stay bare.

mistakes.title: Sealing weep holes and drainage gaps
mistakes.body: Window weep slots, brick weep holes, the bottom of some window flanges and the bottom edges of lap siding are meant to let water out. Seal them and a small leak becomes hidden rot inside the wall. Leave every designed drainage path open.

faqs.q: What is the best caulk for exterior windows?
faqs.a: For painted wood or composite window trim, an elastomeric latex such as DAP Dynaflex 230 or a paintable polymer such as OSI Quad is the best choice. For glass to frame joints and unpainted aluminum or vinyl flanges, use 100 percent silicone such as GE Advanced Silicone 2. Leave weep slots and designed drainage gaps open.

faqs.q: Is silicone or latex better for outdoor caulking?
faqs.a: It depends on whether the joint will be painted. Silicone is more waterproof and UV resistant, but paint will not stick to it and it holds poorly on porous wood and masonry. Elastomeric latex takes paint, cleans up with water and flexes enough for most siding and trim. Use latex on painted wood and silicone on glass and bare metal.

faqs.q: What is the best UV resistant caulk?
faqs.a: Pure silicone is the most UV resistant sealant for unpainted joints, which is why it suits sunny window glass and metal. For joints that will be painted, an elastomeric latex or polymer protected by a coat of exterior acrylic paint holds up well, because the paint shields the sealant from sun and slows the chalking and cracking UV causes.

faqs.q: What is the best paintable caulk for outdoor use?
faqs.a: DAP Dynaflex 230 is the easiest paintable exterior caulk for most homeowners because it cleans up with water and takes latex or oil paint after a short wait. Sashco Big Stretch is the paintable choice for joints that move a lot, and OSI Quad and Geocel 2300 are paintable polymers for vinyl, metal and masonry.

faqs.q: What is the best exterior caulk for wood siding?
faqs.a: An elastomeric latex with an ASTM C920 movement class, such as DAP Dynaflex 230 or Sashco Big Stretch, is the best match for painted wood siding. It grips wood, takes paint and follows the seasonal swelling of long boards. Use backer rod in deep butt joints and replace rotted wood before caulking rather than filling it.

faqs.q: What caulk should I use for holes in exterior metal siding?
faqs.a: Use a solvent-based tripolymer such as Geocel 2300 or a polymer sealant for holes and seams in metal siding, because they bond to metal, stay rubbery and can be painted after cure. If the metal will stay unpainted, 100 percent silicone also works. Clean off rust and oil first, and patch large holes rather than filling them with sealant.

faqs.q: Can I caulk outside in cold weather?
faqs.a: Most water-based caulks need about 40 degrees Fahrenheit or warmer, measured on the surface as well as in the air, and must stay above freezing until they skin over. Some polymer and solvent-based sealants are labeled for colder days. Check the tube, measure shaded walls, and wait if frost or dew may arrive before the bead skins.

bottomLine: DAP Dynaflex 230 is the sensible default for a painted house: easy to gun, paintable and flexible enough for real exterior joints. Move to Sashco Big Stretch where joints keep splitting, OSI Quad Advanced on vinyl and fiber cement, Geocel 2300 on brick and metal, and GE Advanced Silicone 2 on glass and metal that will stay bare. Then do the part that matters most: cut out the old bead, clean to bare surfaces, size deep joints with backer rod, tool the bead and paint when the label allows. A mid-priced tube applied that way will outlast a premium tube laid over old caulk.
